summary:
We took on the challenge "Build a Mission Simulator for Junior Astronauts," designed for ages 8 and up. We developed an interactive game that meets all the challenge requirements, allowing children to design, manage, and simulate their own space mission.

From the start, we built on one key idea: children don’t know the technical concepts used in real missions. So we adapted the content. We simplified the terminology, explained the processes visually, and turned each stage of the mission into a simple, fun activity. The essence of how space exploration works stays intact.

This adaptation is the most important part of our project, because it lets children and young people learn about space missions while they play. It sparks their curiosity about science and technology and makes learning a fun, meaningful experience.
details:
Rocket Space Simulator

What does it do and how does it work?

Rocket Space Simulator is a pixel-art web game for kids ages 8 and up where the player is the engineer of a space mission. Before each launch, they pack their rocket in the hangar with a limited budget, weight, and power. The rocket can carry a heat shield, boosters, food, water, oxygen, medicine, and astronauts. Then they pick a launch site, aim, and launch.

The game has three playable missions, each harder than the one before:

Eye on Earth: one loop around Earth in a 700 km orbit.

Moon Mapper: a 3-day trip to the Moon with two astronauts. The crew lands with a lunar lander, searches for ice, and flies home.

Red Planet Rover: a 7-month cruise to Mars with three astronauts, where water and air must be recycled to last.

When the player makes a mistake, the game shows what went wrong. For example, the rocket burns up without a heat shield, or the crew runs out of oxygen halfway. Then it gives a hint and a real fun fact about that exact mistake, so every failure becomes the lesson.

What benefits does it offer?

It teaches space science through play instead of long lessons. Kids learn by trial and error.

It shows that a real mission is about choices: every kilogram, watt, and credit counts.

It builds critical thinking, planning, and problem-solving skills.

It runs in any web browser with nothing to install, in English and Spanish.

It saves progress and rewards players with stars and ranks, so they want to keep learning.

What is the intended impact?

We want kids everywhere, especially in Latin America, to discover space science and engineering in a fun way and in their own language. We hope it sparks interest in STEM careers and can be used in classrooms, science fairs, and at home. Players learn real facts:

how much food, water, and air an astronaut needs;

why rockets need heat shields;

why water is recycled on the way to Mars.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Languages: JavaScript, HTML, Python and CSS.

Technologies:

React and Vite.

Canvas 2D for the flight maps.

Web Audio for music and sound effects.

The Web Speech API for the trailer's voice, which says the player's name.

i18next for the two languages.

Real science and data:

NASA rates per person per day: 1.83 kg of food, 2.5 kg of water, and 0.84 kg of oxygen.

The 1976 U.S. Standard Atmosphere and aerodynamic heating.

The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.

An Earth–Moon gravity simulation with a moving Moon.

Real launch sites and satellites.

Facts from Apollo and from Perseverance's trip to Mars.

Development: Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub for teamwork, automated tests, and AI coding assistants to support programming.

Hardware: personal computers. Playing only needs a web browser on a computer, tablet, or phone.

How is your project creative?

It turns failure into learning. Each way to lose has its own screen, explanation, and fun fact.

The physics is real but feels simple: kids see their path as dots and drag to aim.

The hangar has trap items that teach players to pack only what they need. Examples are too much fuel, a radio dish that drains power, and plants with no water.

The trailer calls the player by name. On the Moon mission, Laika the space dog shares her story.

The game grows with the player. Each mission needs more astronauts and more supplies, and there is a rocket upgrade that costs credits.

What factors did your team consider?

Age group: short texts, simple sentences, clear colors, and big buttons.

Scientific accuracy: real NASA data, so what kids learn is correct.

Accessibility:

two languages;

layouts for any screen size;

support for the reduced-motion setting.

Performance: smooth play on simple computers.

Motivation: stars, ranks, and missions that unlock one by one.

Balance: every mission can be won by thinking it through, but it is hard enough that mistakes teach something.
